doc.title: Eric Alexander interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, March 31, 2010

chapter: Coming up: Indiana and William Paterson
title: Harold Mabern, 'Embraceable You', and naming favorite tenors
summary: Alexander cannot say what Mabern saw in him; he describes his nervous ballad audition, his new Otto Link mouthpiece, and naming Coltrane, George Coleman and Rollins.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: He must have recognized something in you.
He claims he does. I don’t say this to try to be funny or make the story more interesting, I can’t figure out what he saw in me.

You know there’s a little thing on, I’m not sure whose website it is, if it’s yours or his, it’s somewhere, a little thing about you playing a ballad. He told you to play a ballad, it might have been “Embraceable You.”
Yeah. And he must have, I have to think that he heard something that made him feel like okay this student is worth my while.

Well I can only speculate. I’ll tell you I was very scared, but so ignorant was I, I didn’t know who Harold Mabern was. I mean I could tell that he was somebody super important, but I didn’t know who he was. And I had spent that summer switching from alto saxophone to tenor, and I had just gotten an old Otto Link mouthpiece, which is what I’ve been playing since then, and had to figure out how to play it, and I’d been listening to some Coltrane records kind of trying to approximate that sound. So maybe when I played the melody, so nervous and disoriented was I that I was really taking my time and not overblowing and maybe some little bits of that influence were coming out. It almost could sound like I was patient as opposed to terrified. Maybe that’s what he heard. Well I just had patience. Yeah, there’s a little bit of Coltrane in that sound. You know, and then maybe I was able to get off one or two little melodic ideas that were reminiscent of something. But I do remember him asking me, right after that, he said, “Young man, who are your favorite tenor players?” And I only knew about six. So I said “Coltrane,” and then, for number two, and I didn’t say it necessarily because it was true, it was the first name that came to my mind, I said “George Coleman,” and then I said “Sonny Rollins.” And for him, and see that’s luck again, that’s the perfect answer for him, because he puts Coltrane number one but George Coleman number two and the great Sonny Rollins, of course, everyone loves him, he puts him number three. But unlike most people who put Sonny Rollins and Trane neck and neck, Harold and people that are close to George and love George always put him right after Trane.
